passage: Outside the photo studio in the market, Keerthana held up her phone. "One for the class group," she said. Ayesha checked her reflection in the shop glass and set her lips in the pout she had practised for weeks, a small tilt of the chin, eyes half-lidded. Keerthana clicked. The picture looked polished. A minute later, while Keerthana was scrolling, Ayesha stood at the edge of the pavement, brows pulled together, thumbnail between her teeth. The board results were due the next day. Keerthana glanced up and took a second picture without asking, then showed it. "Which one do you want to post?" Ayesha looked at both. "The first one," she said. "But send me the second."

qa.q: What did Keerthana ask to take a photo for?
qa.a: Keerthana asked for a photo for the class group.

qa.q: What was Ayesha feeling in the second picture, and what else could it be?
qa.a: She looked worried, probably about the board results due the next day, given her pulled brows and thumbnail between her teeth. It could also just be a thinking face, since a single moment is not proof.

qa.q: What would you advise Keerthana about taking a photo without asking?
qa.a: Ask first next time, though she showed Ayesha and let her choose, which was respectful.

qa.q: How might Keerthana have seen Ayesha when she took the second picture?
qa.a: Keerthana may have noticed the change from the polished pout to a tense, worried face, so she captured it and let Ayesha choose which one to post.

grounding: A teenager curates a pout for peers and photos, while a private mood such as worry differs from the public face.

passage:
At the café by the Oslo harbour, Ingrid's friends crowded together for a photo. "Pout face!" someone said. Ingrid tilted her head and pushed her lips out, one eyebrow up, the pose she had practised in the bathroom mirror until it looked effortless.
Snap. The picture looked perfect. Five girls, same pose, all laughing.
But when the others went to order, Ingrid's face dropped. Emil had walked past the window with his new group and hadn't even waved. She stirred her hot chocolate and stared at the foam.
Her friend Maja came back and caught her. "You okay? You looked so happy a second ago."
"That was the photo face," Ingrid said, with a small laugh. "This is the real one."
Maja sat down beside her and slid over half her cinnamon bun.

qa.q: Where had Ingrid practised the pout pose?
qa.a: In the bathroom mirror.

qa.q: What was Ingrid feeling behind the pout, and what shows it?
qa.a: She was feeling hurt and left out because Emil walked past without waving; her face dropping and staring at the foam once the camera was gone shows the pout was for belonging, not her real mood.

qa.q: What did Maja do that helped?
qa.a: Maja noticed the change, asked simply, and stayed close with a small kindness instead of pushing for details.

qa.q: How might Emil see the moment, if he saw it at all?
qa.a: Emil may not have noticed Ingrid in the window at all, and may have no idea the missing wave hurt her.

grounding: A teenager wears a practised pout for a group photo that shows belonging, while her private mood is hurt and quite different.

subtype: Faces shaped for peers and cameras [Regulating]
passage:
On Annual Day, Preeti was the class photographer, moving around backstage with the school camera. Every time she pointed it at Dhruv, he did the same thing: chin down, one side of the mouth pulled up, eyes half-closed. The smirk. Cool, bored, above it all.
"Why do you always do that face?" Preeti asked.
"It's my face," Dhruv said, and did it again.
Ten minutes before his guitar solo, Preeti took a picture without warning. On the screen, Dhruv was sitting on a crate, gripping the guitar neck, lips pressed together, eyes wide.
She showed him. He stared at it a long time.
"Delete that," he said. Then, quieter: "Actually, don't. That's how I actually feel before I go on."
"Nervous?"
"Terrified," he said, and for once he didn't smirk.

qa.q: What was Dhruv gripping in the unplanned photo?
qa.a: The guitar neck.

qa.q: What was Dhruv really feeling behind the smirk?
qa.a: He was terrified before his solo; the smirk was a cool face for peers and the camera that covered his nerves.

qa.q: What could Preeti do next time she catches a real feeling on camera?
qa.a: She could show the person privately first and let them decide whether to keep it, as she did here.

qa.q: How does Preeti see the difference between Dhruv's two faces?
qa.a: Preeti notices the smirk is a pose he repeats for everyone, while the unplanned photo shows a nervous person she had not seen before.

grounding: Backstage at school, a teenager's practised smirk for peers and cameras hides nerves that a candid photo reveals.

passage:
Dear Usha Didi,
You asked why I look the same in every photo. It's the half-smile with my head tilted left. Everyone in my class has a "photo face." Mine took about two weeks to get right.
The truth is, in most of those pictures I'm not happy or sad. I'm just thinking, "Do I look okay? Is my nose weird from this side?" The smile is so I look like I belong in the group.
Last Sunday I found the photo you took at Nani's house when I was laughing at the dog and didn't know you were there. My mouth is crooked and my eyes are tiny. I think it's the best picture of me.
Can you send me the others from that day?
Love,
Pooja

qa.q: How long did Pooja say the photo face took to get right?
qa.a: About two weeks.

qa.q: According to the letter, what is Pooja usually feeling behind the half-smile?
qa.a: Pooja says it's mostly self-consciousness, worrying about looking okay, rather than happiness or sadness; the smile is about belonging with the group.

qa.q: What would you advise Pooja about the photo face?
qa.a: It's fine to keep the photo face with friends, and also worth asking for more candid pictures like the one at Nani's, since Pooja likes how true they look.

qa.q: How might Usha Didi feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Usha Didi might feel touched that Pooja trusts her with this, and glad that her candid photo meant so much.

grounding: In a letter, a teenager explains that a practised photo smile shows belonging and self-consciousness more than real feelings.

passage: Chaitanya, you asked why I always do the same face in photos. Fine, since you're my oldest friend, this is Binita's confession. In Class 8, everyone in our group started doing this half-pout, chin down, one eyebrow up. I practised it in the bathroom mirror for a week. Now it just happens the second a phone comes out. Last month at Riya's birthday I did the pout in every single picture, and everyone commented that I looked so chill. Honestly? I'd had a fight at home that morning and wanted to leave the whole evening. The face was fine. I wasn't. Sometimes I scroll back and I can't tell which photos I was actually happy in. The only one I'm sure about is that blurry one you took, where I'm laughing with rice in my mouth.

qa.q: Where did Binita practise the photo face?
qa.a: In the bathroom mirror, for a week.

qa.q: What was Binita feeling at Riya's birthday behind the pout?
qa.a: Binita felt upset after a fight at home that morning and wanted to leave all evening, even though the photos looked chill.

qa.q: What could Binita try if the practised face starts to feel like a mask?
qa.a: Keep some unposed photos and tell a close friend like Chaitanya how the day really went, instead of letting the face do all the talking.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya see the blurry photo?
qa.a: Chaitanya may see it as the truest picture of Binita, catching real laughter instead of the practised face.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager's practised photo face signalling belonging while the private mood underneath is different.
